text.p: Negotiators for the United Steelworkers of America and Wheeling-Pittsburgh Corp. said Sunday they reached a tentative five-year contract settling the union's 10-month old strike.

Concessions won by Wheeling-Pittsbugh, a unit of WHX Corp., include cutting the workforce, through attrition, by 850 workers company-wide over next 18 months, and enhanced flexibility with work rules.

The union negotiators won a return to a defined benefit pension, which is common in the steel industry. It gives $40 a month in benefits for each year of service, and rises in value to $44 a month on June 1, 2003.
The pension plan includes benefits for retirement at age 55 with 30 years of service, and shutdown benefits to be paid in the event of a departmental or plant closing.
The accord gives $1.50 an hour in wage increases, a $2,000 signing bonus, and sets aside $2 million to reimburse workers for medical expenses incurred during the strike.
The contract was approved Sunday by a majority of the eight local union presidents. Ballots will be sent to the union's 4,500 striking members by the end of the week.
The 850 cut workers will be eligble for enhanced pensions that include full benefits, along with a choice of a lump sum payment of $25,000, or $400 in monthly supplemental payments until age 62.
"This contract is a testament to the solidarity of the 4,500 steelworkers and their families who endured 10 grueling months," said Jim Bowen, chairman of the USWA negotiating committee.

WHX Corp. has also agreed to reopen two of the four plants closed during the strike, which began Oct. 1. The Beech Bottom plant in Beech Bottom, W. Va., and the roofing operations at the Martins Ferry, Ohio, plant will reopen.
The LaBelle Works in Wheeling, W. Va., which was sold during the strike, and a small plant in Grand Junction, Colo., will not return to operation.
Although the contract was passed by the union presidents, it did not pass unanimously. The union would not disclose the breakdown of the vote.

Mickey Forte, president of Local 1187 in Allenport, Pa., was one of the dissenting votes. "We're happy to get the pensions, but we're not happy with the amount of jobs being lost. You can word it anyway you want to, but we're still losing 850 jobs," he said.
The contract would run from the date of ratification until Sept. 1, 2002. The pension provisions continue until expiration of the successor labour agreement.
No date has been set for the vote.
